title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render
summary:
You can now stream generative UI from your Chat SDK agent with json-render.

With a typed catalog of components, the agent writes a JSON spec that json-render converts into a Chat SDK card. Each adapter then posts the card in its platform’s native format, such as Block Kit on Slack and Adaptive Cards on Teams.

The catalog covers tables, charts, buttons, and more, so there’s no separate tool to build and maintain for each message shape.

Stream cards as the model writes

streamCard posts the card once its root element has content and updates the message as new elements stream in. Edits go out at most once every 500 ms by default, which matches Chat SDK’s streaming interval. Once the stream ends, the message shows the final, validated card.

Validate specs and enforce platform limits

toCard checks every element’s props against its component schema and throws CardSpecError for an invalid spec. Each problem gets its own readable issue, so you can send the list back to the model for a corrected spec.

Platforms cap what a single message can hold, and Chat SDK adapters degrade content past those caps. The Slack adapter, for example, turns a second table into a code block. Pass limits to reject those specs instead.

Read the documentation to get started, or try the playground.

Run vercel deploy with --delete-project-after and a duration:

title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
summary:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect , and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.

title: Token Pass credit now applies automatically across AI Gateway
summary:
Token Pass credit now applies automatically to included model usage through AI Gateway, whether a request authenticates with an API key, OIDC token, or fx login. title: Ampersand from Humans& now available on AI Gateway
summary:
Ampersand from Humans& is now available on AI Gateway for free through November 13, 2026.

Ampersand is a model for group conversations. Humans& built Ampersand on Z.ai's open-weight GLM 5.3 and trained it with reinforcement learning in simulated group conversations that run for up to months of simulated time. Most chat models are built for one person asking a question and the model answering it. Ampersand is trained to take part in a conversation between several people. It reads every message, including the ones not addressed to it, and after each one it decides whether to reply or stay quiet.

It is designed to understand individual and shared goals, help people work through disagreements, and recognize when a contribution would be useful. That can mean asking a clarifying question, sharing relevant context, or waiting while people respond to one another.

For example:

Sam: Heads up, I'm out Friday, driving to my sister's. Alex: Have a good trip! Maya: Let's do the launch rehearsal Friday at 10 with all three of us. Ampersand: Quick flag, Maya: Sam said he's out Friday driving to his sister's, so a Friday 10am rehearsal with all three probably won't work. Might be worth picking a different time so everyone can make it.

Your application exposes these actions as caller-defined function tools. send_message delivers a contribution, while pass leaves the conversation quiet until the next human message. Your application executes both tools and records their results.

title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
summary:
The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race.

Subscribe to messages inside the run

The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null.

Idempotency with no extra code

The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally.

Setting experimental_minRetention keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from start(), so late duplicates are still refused.

Upgrade to workflow 5.4.0 and read the idempotency documentation to get started.

title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
summary:
Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems.

You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time.

We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying.

What are Vercel Schedules?

Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs, but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work.

You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs:

  • Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy. You can use them to call private functions or HTTP paths, or send messages to Queue topics.

  • Dynamic schedules let your app create and manage schedules through the JS SDK, CLI, or API as it runs. They support one-time and recurring work through Queue topics.

You can also test scheduled work on Preview deployments and in custom environments before running it in Production.

How Schedules works

Take this example: A user could ask an agent with web access, “Tomorrow morning, summarize the top five stories on Hacker News.” The traditional solution would be storing the request and its schedule time in a database, then using a cron job to check for work that is due.

With Schedules, an agent can create a schedule that records the request and when to run it, without a separate database and polling job. The example below defines an AI SDK tool that gives an agent this capability.

When the task is due, Vercel uses Queues to deliver the saved request to your app. Your app provides code to read that request, check the user’s current permissions, and start the agent. The agent fetches the top five Hacker News posts with a web tool, then returns a summary for your app to save for the user.

If you already build agents with fx’s JavaScript library, libfx or Pi’s agent library, you can add a similar scheduling tool. The eve agent framework uses Vercel Schedules to provide dynamic scheduling tools for production agents hosted on Vercel.

Run recurring application jobs

You can schedule recurring work with Vercel Schedules. Schedules can be created dynamically via the JS SDK, API, and CLI, or set up in your project’s configuration.

For example, to create a job that cleans up expired records every day, you could define a schedule that invokes a private function in your chosen time zone:

Vercel calls this cleanup code directly, without exposing it at a public URL. It checks that each call comes from the scheduling service, so you don’t have to add that check yourself.

If your app already uses the Nitro 3 server framework, its experimental integration lets you run the recurring jobs in your existing scheduledTasks configuration as private functions.

You can also try the agent task and cleanup locally with vercel dev, then test them on a Preview branch or in a custom environment before production. Use Run Schedule in your project’s Schedules tab to try either task without waiting, and see when past runs happened.

Get started

Vercel Schedules is now in Public Beta, and you can use it for the recurring tasks your application already runs. When a user or agent chooses when work should happen, your code can create and manage a schedule for that task.

To get started, check out the Vercel Schedules skill and read the documentation.

title: Vercel token scanning expands to more public sources
summary:
Vercel has partnered with Truffle Security to expand automated detection and revocation of publicly exposed Vercel tokens.

Revoking exposed credentials helps prevent unauthorized access to your projects and unexpected costs from unauthorized use of services such as Vercel Sandbox and Vercel AI Gateway. If your token is revoked, you’ll receive an email from us explaining why.

Truffle Security reports tokens exposed in public sources including GitHub, GitLab, Docker, npm, PyPI, Hugging Face, Android APKs, and Firefox Add-ons. Vercel has revoked hundreds of tokens reported by Truffle Security.

A separate Vercel scanner now checks each new monthly Common Crawl dataset of public web pages and automatically revokes any exposed Vercel tokens it finds.

Learn more about creating tokens, setting their scopes, and managing them in the access token documentation.

title: Vercel Security Review now in public beta
summary:
Vercel Security Review is now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Once enabled, every push to a connected GitHub repository is automatically reviewed for vulnerabilities, and findings are reported in the Vulnerabilities dashboard.

What triggers a review

Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, direct and force pushes to your production branch are reviewed as well. Every project affected by a single push is reviewed together.

What a finding includes

Each finding records the project, environment, branch, and commit, with a summary, a suggested fix, and an AI-generated severity rating.

Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. When there's a pull request, it also posts findings as review comments that link back to each finding. On public repositories, finding details stay in the dashboard.

Fixes and resolution

Clicking Fix with Vercel Agent on a vulnerability report hands the finding to Vercel Agent, which proposes a fix and opens a pull request for you to review. Nothing merges until you approve it.

To fix findings with your coding agent instead, use vercel security vulnerabilities in the Vercel CLI, or copy any finding as Markdown or JSON.

Security policies

Teams can write security policies in plain language, for all projects or specific ones, to give Security Review more context about how they build. Set a team policy in Agent settings and a project policy in the project's Security settings.

Limitations

Security Review analyzes source code. It isn't a security audit, and it doesn't perform runtime or penetration testing. It helps you find vulnerabilities but doesn't guarantee your application is free of them.

Pricing

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate: provider inference at the underlying token rate with no markup, plus the Vercel Token Rate of $0.25 per million tokens (input, cached, output). Reviews run on each push to GitHub, so cost scales with how often you push and how much code changes.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026, and fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the Vercel Agent rate.

Enable Security Review in your team’s Agent settings, or read the documentation and the announcement to learn more. The CLI command needs Vercel CLI 65.10.0 or later.

title: Vercel CI no longer requires a linked Vercel project
summary:
Vercel CI can now run on a GitHub repository that has no Vercel project. Until now you had to create an empty project just to connect the repository.

To enable it, you need:

  • The Vercel GitHub App installed with access to the repository

  • Your GitHub account connected to your Vercel account

  • Write or admin permission on the repository

Then, from a clone of the repository, run:

CI is enabled for the team your CLI is set to. Pass --scope to use a different one. From the next push, tasks run as configured in your repository.

Private GitHub repositories only. Public repositories and other Git providers are not yet supported.

Read the Vercel CI documentation to configure tasks.

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
summary:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.

title: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
summary:
Mercor on Vercel

  • Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours

  • 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days

  • Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport

  • Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders

Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises.

Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

What’s next

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

About Mercor: Mercor is an AI data company that organizes human intelligence for AI training and evaluation. Its network of more than 5M experts, from doctors to lawyers to engineers, powers benchmarks, enterprise evals, RL environments, post-training and agent deployments.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
summary:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. title: Vercel MCP now supports Client ID Metadata Documents
summary:
Any MCP client can now ask to connect to Vercel MCP. You still log in and approve each connection, but the client no longer has to be reviewed by Vercel first. Previously, Vercel reviewed and allowlisted each client and its redirect URIs by hand, and anything not on the list was rejected.

To connect, a client publishes a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), a JSON file on its own domain that describes it, and uses that file's HTTPS URL as its OAuth client_id. This follows the MCP authorization spec, which now recommends CIMD over Dynamic Client Registration.

Because Vercel hasn't reviewed these clients, the consent screen shows where each one comes from: its name, its logo, and the hostname that serves its metadata document, for example "Claude Code by claude.ai". CIMD clients don't get the Vercel verified badge, so the hostname is what you're trusting when you approve.

Apps already registered with Vercel are unchanged.

Read the Vercel MCP documentation to connect your client.

title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
summary:
Today, we are launching Vercel Security Review in public beta.

Security Review is a new capability in Vercel Agent, alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories.

Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings.

How it works

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works:

  1. You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project.

  2. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets.

  3. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request.

  4. You can fix findings by clicking Fix with Vercel Agent in the dashboard, or use the CLI to pull findings and have your own coding agent implement changes.

  5. When subsequent security reviews no longer detect a finding, it is marked as no longer detected in the dashboard, and the GitHub comment is closed.

Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment.

What the agent checks

The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. That process is how it catches logic flaws like missing authorization checks, which pattern-matching scanners miss.

Each review also applies your team’s security policies, which you can write in plain language and apply to specific projects or across your team. For example, a policy can require any endpoint that returns customer data to check that the requester owns it. You can also manage policies with the Vercel CLI, using vercel security policy.

How findings are tracked

Each new finding is checked against ones that have already been reported, so the same issue isn’t flagged twice. Every finding is tied to the deployment where it first appeared and changes are followed from there. That means that when a vulnerable change from a pull request is merged into your production branch, the finding is flagged in production as well.

When a later review no longer detects the issue in an environment, the agent marks the finding as no longer detected there.

Acting on findings

Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared.

Findings are listed in the Vulnerability view in the Security dashboard, where you can ask Vercel Agent to validate and commit fixes. Findings are also available via CLI, so you can fix vulnerabilities with your own coding agent.

Each new finding generates an audit log event, which Enterprise teams can send to their SIEM through Audit Log Drains.

Here is a demo of sample findings in the dashboard:

Fixing vulnerabilities with Vercel Agent

When Vercel Agent can fix a finding, you will see the option to click Fix with Vercel Agent on the finding page in the dashboard. After you click, the agent confirms the vulnerability still exists, then makes the smallest change that fixes it and updates the tests.

Say a developer pushes a change to an invoice download endpoint, and the lookup doesn't check which organization the invoice belongs to. Within seconds, Security Review flags that any signed-in user could download another organization's invoice by changing its ID. Vercel Agent's fix scopes the lookup to the user's organization:

Fixing vulnerabilities with your own coding agent

You can point your coding agent or other systems at the Vercel CLI to pull and fix vulnerabilities:

Findings in the dashboard also give you the ability to copy details as Markdown or JSON, making it easy to paste them into an agent conversation.

Every code change needs security review

Frontier AI models are making vulnerabilities far easier to find and exploit. Last month, researchers turned two decade-old flaws in PHP core into working remote code execution exploits with relatively little effort.

How it works

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works:

  1. You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project.

  2. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets.

  3. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request.

title: Blocking malicious npm packages before and during installation
summary:
Vercel now checks for blocked npm packages before and during dependency installation in builds, helping prevent malicious install scripts from running.

The checks use a blocklist of specific package versions selected for blocking because of malware or security vulnerabilities, with new rules typically reaching new builds within minutes.

  • Before installation, Vercel checks supported lockfiles, including when dependencies are restored from the build cache.

  • During installation, Vercel blocks affected public npm downloads.

Existing checks of installed dependencies and function outputs continue before deployment.

These protections apply automatically to new builds on all plans, with no configuration required.

If a blocked dependency is detected, Vercel fails the deployment, identifies the package and version in the error, and attempts to invalidate the affected build cache. Update the dependency to a safe version and update the lockfile, then redeploy.

title: Introducing Geist Serif
summary:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.
